title: Friends, Advisers and the Tongue
sum: Ben Sira turns to the people we lean on. Some friends are friends in name only and turn against us in trouble (37:1-6). Advisers often advise for their own gain, so the reader should find out what they want, avoid asking anyone whose interest runs against the advice, stay close to a godly man, trust the counsel of his own heart, and above all pray to the Most High (37:7-15).

A short poem on words follows: every work begins with a word, and the tongue rules over good and evil, life and death (37:16-18). Four kinds of wise men are compared by whom their wisdom serves, and the best is the one who teaches his people, whose name lives forever (37:19-26). The chapter ends with practical health advice: test what is good for you and do not overeat (37:27-31), which leads into the praise of doctors in chapter 38.
readings: Read as practical advice

Most of the chapter is common sense: check motives, choose good company, trust your judgment, eat moderately. Its examples (the rival wife, the merchant, the lazy servant) come from daily life in Jerusalem, and its advice still works.
Read as faith at work
The advice is framed by God: the godly friend "keeps the commandments" (37:12), and after all human counsel "ask the Most High" (37:15). Read this way, prudence is part of piety, not a rival to it.

views.C: For Catholic readers, who count Sirach as Scripture, the chapter joins prudence, good counsel and prayer, and ends by sending the reader to the Most High (37:15).
views.P: Protestants, who do not count Sirach as Scripture, find in this chapter the same wisdom as Proverbs 11:14 and Proverbs 15:22 on advisers, and James 3 on the tongue.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D survives for the whole chapter and often differs from the Greek, as at 37:3, 37:5, 37:8 and 37:17-18. The Hebrew is hard in places, and the notes give its readings beside the Greek.
views.J: In the Hebrew of 37:3 evil asks, "Why was I formed so?" The verb for "formed" (notsarti) is from the root of yetser, the word later rabbis used for the inclination to evil.

echoes: Proverbs 18:24; Proverbs 11:14; Proverbs 15:22; Proverbs 16:33; Deuteronomy 30:15; Proverbs 18:21; James 3:5–6; Mark 14:34; Numbers 11:20

settings.what: Teaching on friends, advisers, the tongue, the wise and eating
settings.to: "My child" (37:27): his pupils, young men who would soon run households and offices
settings.when: In the second half of the book, before the praise of the doctor (38:1-15)
settings.why: To teach them whom to trust, how to weigh advice and how to live long. Knowing the hearers were young men entering public life explains the stress on advisers who use you for their own ends, and on the wise man whose name lives in Israel.
settings.readers: For chapters 37-43 as a whole: Ben Sira's own pupils in Jerusalem, about 180 BC (the date Rendsburg and Binstein give for the book); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, where his grandson arrived in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes, 132 BC, and translated the book (the prologue; Rendsburg and Binstein). For this chapter: its Hebrew survives in two medieval copies from the Cairo Genizah, manuscripts B and D, so Jews were still copying this teaching in the Middle Ages.
views: A school for young men

Ben Sira addresses "my child" and invites the untaught to his "house of instruction" (51:23), so the book can be read as teaching for pupils from Jerusalem families who would serve as scribes, judges and officials.
A book for any household
The advice also covers family, money, health and mourning, so it can be read as meant for any devout Jewish household that could read or hear it.

title: The Doctor, the Mourner and the Workers
sum: The chapter opens with a long praise of doctors. The Lord created the doctor and the remedies that come from the earth; a sensible person will not refuse them, any more than Moses refused the wood that sweetened the water (38:1-8). When sick, the believer should pray, turn from sin and bring an offering, and then give the doctor his place, since doctors too pray for success (38:9-15).

Ben Sira then teaches how to mourn: weep, lament and bury the dead properly, but limit grief, since it can kill, and there is no way back from death (38:16-23). Finally he begins his comparison of the scholar with the workers. The farmer, the craftsman, the smith and the potter give their hearts to their work and lie awake over it. The city could not stand without them, but they have no time for the wisdom that rules in the assembly and the court (38:24-34).
readings: Read as a defense of medicine

Ben Sira says medicine is God's own provision: the Lord created the doctor and the remedies (38:1, 4, 12), and the doctor too prays (38:14). Prayer and the doctor belong together. Whether he meant to answer a suspicion like the Chronicler's verdict on Asa (2 Chronicles 16:12) is Claude's suggestion, in the box below.
Read as a lesson in order

The order matters: God first, then repentance and worship, then the doctor. Healing is from the Most High (38:2), working through means he created. On this reading the passage teaches dependence on God in every step, not a split between faith and medicine.
Read as social portrait

The trades passage gives a vivid picture of Hellenistic Judea: farmers, seal-cutters, smiths and potters at work. Ben Sira honors their skill but keeps public wisdom for the scribe, a view some readers find narrow.

views.C: The Catechism teaches that "Life and physical health are precious gifts entrusted to us by God. We must take reasonable care of them" (Catechism 2288). Sirach 38 joins prayer and the doctor.
views.P: Protestants who do not count Sirach as Scripture agree with its balance from the New Testament: Jesus says the sick need a doctor (Matthew 9:12), Luke was "the beloved doctor" (Colossians 4:14), and Paul recommends wine for the stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).
views.H: The chapter makes room within Israel's faith for medicine. The trades passage has the same plan as the Egyptian Satire of the Trades (see the note at 38:25).
views.J: Genesis Rabbah 10:6 quotes "Bar Sira" on the medicines God brings from the earth. The Talmud learns from Exodus 21:19 that a doctor has permission to heal (see the medicine page).

deep.h: The Greek and the Hebrew of 38:1-15
deep.b: Manuscript B of the Cairo Genizah preserves most of the physician passage in Hebrew, and it differs from the Greek in telling ways. It begins "Make a friend of the doctor before you need him" (38:1, Hebrew). It says "God brings out remedies from the earth" (38:4, Hebrew), the form Genesis Rabbah quotes in Ben Sira's name. It tells the sick to offer the grain offering with the Leviticus word 'azkarah and to give as much as their means allow (38:11). And it ends, "Whoever sins before his Maker will act defiantly before the doctor" (38:15, Hebrew), where the Greek wishes the sinner into the doctor's hands. The margin of manuscript B has a second reading close to the Greek. The Greek is the text the churches received; the Hebrew shows a warmer view of the doctor still.

From 38:24 to 39:11 Ben Sira compares the scribe with four workers: the plowman, the craftsman and seal-cutter, the smith and the potter. Each "gives his heart" to his task and "lies awake" over it. None has time to study the law or to judge. Yet Ben Sira does not despise them. "Each one is wise in his own work" (38:31), no city could stand without them (38:32), and "their prayer is in the work of their craft" (38:34). The comparison ends with the scribe, who "gives his heart" to rising early to pray (39:5). The Egyptian Satire of the Trades sets the scribe against the trades in the same way, and Egyptologists disagree whether it mocks them; Ben Sira's version is plainly respectful (see the note at 38:25).

deep.title: Claude's theory: an answer to King Asa
deep.b: My suggestion: Ben Sira's physician passage reads like a reply to the Chronicler's verdict on Asa, who "did not seek the LORD, only the healers" (2 Chronicles 16:12). Ben Sira keeps what the Chronicler cared about, seeking the Lord first (38:9-11), and removes the suspicion of doctors by saying the Lord created them (38:1, 12). A Jerusalem scribe who studied "the law, the prophets and the other books" (the prologue) would likely have known Chronicles. I have not found this connection argued in a source I could check, so it remains my own reading.

echoes: Exodus 15:23–26; 2 Chronicles 16:12; Leviticus 2:1–3; James 5:14–16; Matthew 9:12; Colossians 4:14; 2 Samuel 12:23; Job 7:9; Ezra 7:6–10; Jeremiah 18:3–6; Exodus 31:3–5

settings.to: His pupils, and through them every household that falls sick
settings.why: To give doctors and medicine an honored place in a life of faith, so that no one thinks seeking a doctor means distrusting God. Knowing that the hearers were devout men who prayed and brought offerings at the Temple explains the order he gives: prayer, repentance and an offering first, then the doctor.
settings.readers: Manuscript B of the Cairo Genizah keeps nearly all of this passage in Hebrew, and Genesis Rabbah 10:6 quotes its teaching on remedies from the earth in the name of "Bar Sira," so the rabbis knew it.
views: Against suspicion of doctors

Read on its own terms, the passage answers anyone who thinks that seeking a doctor means distrusting God: the Lord created the doctor (38:1, 12). That Ben Sira had the Chronicler's verdict on Asa in mind (2 Chronicles 16:12) is Claude's suggestion (see the box).
Prayer first
The passage also puts prayer, repentance and an offering before the doctor (38:9-12), so it can be read as a call to trust God in medicine, not instead of it.

settings.to: "My child" (38:16): pupils who would one day bury parents and friends
settings.why: To make sure the dead are honored and buried properly, and to keep the living from being destroyed by grief, since there is no return from death.
settings.readers: Manuscript B keeps this teaching on mourning in Hebrew, all but 38:19.

settings.to: His pupils, who were training to be scribes
settings.when: The center of the book's second half
settings.why: To show the dignity and the cost of the scholar's calling: it needs freedom from manual work and gives a lasting name, but it rests on the labor of others, whom the scholar must honor. Knowing that the hearers were trainee scribes explains why the trades are described from the outside, with respect but not envy.
settings.readers: Manuscript B keeps the Hebrew of 38:24-27, then has nothing until 39:15, and no other Hebrew copy of the portrait of the scribe is known. Later readers knew it in Greek and Latin.
views: A self-portrait
Ben Sira signs his book as its author (50:27) and calls his pupils to his "house of instruction" (51:23), so 39:1-11 can be read as his own ideal and his own life.
A school text
The passage has the same plan as the Egyptian Satire of the Trades (see the note at 38:25), so it can also be read as a standard piece of scribal teaching, reshaped.

title: The Scholar and the Hymn of Good Works
sum: The portrait of the scribe reaches its height. He gives his soul to the law of the Most High, the wisdom of the ancients and the prophecies, and to proverbs and parables. He serves rulers and travels abroad. Above all he rises at dawn to pray, and if God wills, a spirit of understanding fills him. His name will live from generation to generation (39:1-11).

Then Ben Sira calls his pupils to sing and gives them a hymn (39:12-35). Its refrain is that the Lord's works are all good, and no one may ask "What is this for?" Everything was made for its purpose and its time. The good things of life are good for the godly and harmful to sinners, and even winds, hail, famine, beasts and the sword were made to punish and obey him gladly. The hymn ends in a call to bless the name of the Lord.
readings: Read as an answer to the problem of evil
The hymn faces the existence of harmful things and answers that they serve God's justice in their time. It is a confident answer, closer to Proverbs and Deuteronomy than to Job.
Read as worship
The hymn does not argue so much as praise. Its refrains are meant to be sung, and its answer is the answer of trust: what we cannot explain still has its place in a good creation (Ecclesiastes 3:11).

views.C: Catholic readers find in 39:1-11 a picture of the teacher who joins study and prayer, and in the hymn the teaching that all creation is good (compare 1 Timothy 4:4).
views.P: Protestant readers compare the scribe with Ezra (Ezra 7:10) and the hymn with Psalm 104 and Romans 8:28.
views.H: The Hebrew of manuscript B survives from 39:15, and scraps of the Masada scroll, copied in the first century BC, from 39:27. Between 38:28 and 39:14 no Hebrew is known.
views.J: The hymn's confidence that everything has its time and purpose is close to Ecclesiastes 3:1-11, and its call to bless the Name (39:35) uses the language of Jewish prayer.

deep.b: The hymn is built on three refrains. "The Lord's works, every one of them, are (very) good" opens and closes it (39:16, 33). "No one may say" comes three times (39:17, 21, 34). Between them Ben Sira lists the good necessities of life (39:26) and the harmful things (39:28-30). His answer has two parts. First, everything has its time: what looks useless now "will be sought out in its own time" (39:17). Second, the same things work good for the godly and harm for sinners (39:25-27). Job and Ecclesiastes would ask whether that is always so (Job 21:7; Ecclesiastes 7:15), and Paul later says that "all things work together toward good for those who love God" (Romans 8:28), a promise rather than a rule of nature. Ben Sira's answer is offered as praise, and it ends in blessing.

deep.h: The first scraps of the Masada scroll
deep.b: Column I of the Masada scroll, copied in the first century BC (the NETS introduction), keeps only the ends of a few lines of 39:27-32, a few letters each. At 39:28 it has ים יע, a gap, and יקו with a doubtful ת before it, letters that fit the verb "they move" (ya'atiqu) that manuscript B keeps there. At 39:29 it has only ראו; its editor restores "were created" (nibre'u). The scraps are too small to prove much, but where they can be read they are compatible with manuscript B, a medieval copy.

echoes: Ezra 7:6–10; Proverbs 1:6; Genesis 1:31; Exodus 15:8; Psalm 33:7; Psalm 107:34; Psalm 148:8; Ecclesiastes 3:11; Romans 8:28; 1 Timothy 4:4

settings.what: The hymn: all the Lord's works are good
settings.to: "You holy sons" (39:13): his pupils, called to sing it
settings.when: After the portrait of the scribe; it puts into practice the scribe's praise (39:6)
settings.why: To teach the young to praise God for creation and to trust that even harmful things serve his purpose. For pupils who would meet suffering and unjust powers, the hymn gives a way to hold faith and hard experience together.
settings.readers: Manuscript B keeps the hymn from 39:15. The Masada scroll, copied in the first century BC (the NETS introduction), keeps scraps of 39:27-32 in its first column, so Jews were copying this hymn before the Christian era.

title: Human Misery and What Is Better
sum: Ben Sira turns to the burden of human life. From the king on his throne to the poor man in raw linen, every person carries fears, quarrels and bad dreams, and sinners suffer seven times more (40:1-11). Then he names what lasts: bribes and injustice pass away, but faithfulness, kindness and almsgiving remain (40:12-17).

A chain of nine sayings follows (ten in the Hebrew of manuscript B), each naming two good things and then a third "better than both": a good wife, the love of wisdom, a pleasant tongue, almsgiving, good counsel, and at the top the fear of the Lord, which is like a paradise of blessing (40:18-27). The chapter ends with a warning against living off other people's tables: "It is better to die than to beg" (40:28-30).
readings: Read as realism
Ben Sira does not pretend life is easy. Like Job and Ecclesiastes he names the weariness of toil and the fear of death, and he gives no cheap comfort.
Read as a ladder of values

The "better than both" sayings teach the young how to rank the goods of life, with the fear of the Lord at the top. Read this way, the misery of 40:1-11 is the setting for a wise choice of what lasts.

views.C: Catholic readers link the praise of almsgiving (40:17, 24) to the Church's teaching on works of mercy, discussed on the almsgiving page.
views.P: Protestant readers find the same honesty about toil and death in Job 7:1 and Ecclesiastes 1:13, and read the chain of sayings as wisdom like Proverbs 15:16-17.
views.H: The Greek and the Hebrew of manuscript B often differ in this chapter (40:1, 40:11, 40:17, 40:18, 40:20, 40:27), and the Masada scroll sides now with one, now with the other.
views.J: The margin of manuscript B, beside 40:22-23, writes a saying that the Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes in Ben Sira's name: "All the days of the poor are evil. Ben Sira says: even the nights."

echoes: Genesis 3:17–20; Job 1:21; Job 7:1; Ecclesiastes 1:13; Ecclesiastes 1:7; Genesis 6:13; Proverbs 10:2; Tobit 12:9; Isaiah 4:5; Proverbs 15:15; Proverbs 19:14

settings.what: On human misery, what lasts, and begging
settings.when: After the hymn on God's good works (39:12-35)
settings.why: To set the goodness of creation beside the hard facts of human life, and to teach what is worth seeking. For young men who might be tempted by bribes, easy wealth or a patron's table, the chapter says what lasts and what shames.
settings.readers: Manuscript B keeps the chapter in Hebrew, and the Masada scroll has scraps from 40:8 and much of 40:11-30. The Talmud quotes in Ben Sira's name (Sanhedrin 100b) the saying on the poor that B writes in its margin beside 40:22-23.

title: O Death, and a Good Name
sum: Two short poems address death. It is bitter to the man at ease and welcome to the old and worn out, but it is the Lord's sentence on all flesh, and in Hades no one argues over how long a life was (41:1-4). The children of the ungodly inherit disgrace, and those who abandon the law of the Most High are born and die under a curse (41:5-10).

Against this Ben Sira sets a good name, which lasts longer than gold and outlives the body (41:11-13). Then he begins a long lesson on shame: there is shame that guards from sin and shame that should be set aside. He lists what to be ashamed of before parents, rulers, judges, the congregation, friends and neighbors, from sexual sin and lies to bad table manners and taunting a friend after giving him a gift (41:14-22).
readings: Read as the wisdom of the Old Testament
Ben Sira looks at death without the hope of resurrection. His comfort is a good name and the life of Israel. Read this way, the chapter shows the faith of Israel before Daniel 12 and the Maccabees.
Read as a challenge to the reader
The poems are not only about death but about how to live: accept the Lord's sentence, keep the law, guard your name, know what to be ashamed of.

views.C: For Catholic readers, 41:1-4 belongs to a canon that also includes the Wisdom of Solomon and 2 Maccabees, where hope beyond death is clearer (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1-4; 2 Maccabees 7:9).
views.O: Orthodox readers, with the same wider Old Testament, read Ben Sira's silence about the afterlife beside the Wisdom of Solomon's hope for the righteous.
views.P: Protestants note that Ben Sira's view of Hades matches Ecclesiastes 9:10 and Psalm 6:5, books in their canon, and that the New Testament goes beyond both.
views.H: The woe on those who abandon the law (41:8) can be read in the light of the pull of Greek ways in Jerusalem that 1 Maccabees describes (1 Maccabees 1:11-15).
views.J: The Hebrew of 41:11, "A human being is a vapor (hevel) in his body, but a name of loyal love will not be cut off," uses the key word of Ecclesiastes.

deep.b: Ben Sira often speaks of death. He knows it is God's sentence (41:3-4), that it brings no return (38:21), that in Hades no one praises God (17:27-28) and no one argues about the length of a life (41:4). He does not mention the resurrection hope of Daniel 12:2. What lasts is a good name (41:11-13), children (40:19), and the life of Israel, whose days "cannot be counted" (37:25). The Masada scroll and manuscript B show that the Hebrew said the same. For readers of the New Testament, Ben Sira is a faithful witness to the question that Easter answers (1 Corinthians 15:55).

echoes: Job 21:23–26; Ecclesiastes 9:10; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 90:4; Genesis 5:27; Hebrews 9:27; 1 Maccabees 1:11–15; Deuteronomy 28:15–19; Ecclesiastes 7:1; Proverbs 22:1; 1 Corinthians 15:55

settings.what: On death and a good name
settings.to: His pupils and every reader facing death
settings.when: After the teaching on human misery (40:1-11)
settings.why: To help the young accept death as God's sentence without fear, and to give them a reason to live well: a good name lasts.
settings.readers: Both manuscript B and the Masada scroll (columns II-III) keep these poems on death in Hebrew.

settings.to: "Ungodly men, who have abandoned the law of God Most High" (41:8), named in a woe, though those who heard it were his pupils
settings.when: Inside the poems on death and a good name (41:1-13)
settings.why: To warn the pupils, by a woe spoken over others, that leaving the law brings a curse in birth and in death (41:9-10). Knowing that the people named are not the people in the room shows the woe is a warning, not a sentence on the hearers.
settings.readers: The Masada scroll (column III) keeps the end of 41:8, "who forsake the law of the Most High," in Hebrew.
views: Jews drawn to Greek ways
The woe can be read against the Jerusalem renegades of 1 Maccabees 1:11-15, who wanted to make a covenant with the nations (see the note at 41:8).
The ungodly in every age
It can also be read as a general woe, like the contrast of the two ways in Psalm 1.

settings.when: The Hebrew opens it with a heading, "Listen, children, to instruction about shame"
settings.why: To teach a sense of shame that guards against sin, and the courage not to be ashamed of doing right. For young men in a society that prized honor, the lesson set God's law above public opinion.
settings.readers: The Masada scroll (columns III-IV) and manuscript B keep this lesson in Hebrew, and both open it with the heading "instruction about shame" (41:14).

title: What Not to Be Ashamed Of, and the Works of God
sum: Ben Sira lists what a person should do without shame: keep God's law, judge fairly, settle accounts honestly, keep scales true, discipline children, guard property and put every transaction in writing (42:1-8). Then he describes a father's worry over a daughter at each stage of life, and gives harsh advice and one of his harshest lines about women (42:9-14).

At 42:15 the book turns to the great hymn on God's works in creation. God made all by his word; the sun shines on everything, full of his glory; not even the angels can tell all his wonders. He searches the deep and the heart, knows past and future, needs no counselor, and made all things in pairs, each making the other's good stronger (42:15-25).
readings: Read in its own world
The advice on daughters reflects a society where a family's honor depended on its daughters' marriages. Read in that world, it is a father's anxiety, harshly expressed.
Read against the rest of the Bible

Lines like 42:14 conflict with the Bible's praise of good women and with the equality of men and women before God (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28). Readers who hold Sirach as Scripture and those who do not both have to weigh it.
Read as the start of a hymn
From 42:15 the chapter belongs with chapter 43: a hymn on creation that leads into the Praise of the Fathers (44-50), God's works in nature and then in history.

views.C: The Catholic weekday lectionary reads 42:15-25 on Thursday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I, lectionary 350).
views.P: Protestant readers compare the hymn with Psalm 104 and Job 38-39, books in every Christian Bible.
views.H: The Masada scroll preserves 41:21-42:14 and most of 42:15-25 in columns IV and V. It writes 'adonai, "Lord," where manuscript B has 'elohim or the abbreviation of the divine name.
views.J: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes a form of the daughter passage in Ben Sira's name, as one reason some rabbis hesitated over the book.

deep.b: The Ben Sira scroll from Masada, the desert fortress by the Dead Sea, was found in Yigael Yadin's excavations of 1963-1965 and published by him in 1965 (Corley's bibliography). It was copied in the first century BC (the NETS introduction) and has much of 39:27-44:17 (Corley). Each line holds one couplet, with a space between its halves, as Eric Reymond's transcription shows. It agrees with the medieval manuscript B often enough to show that B preserves an ancient text, and it differs often enough to show that the Hebrew was still changing. In this part its readings appear in the variants and notes at 40:17, 40:18, 40:27, 41:2, 41:8, 41:10-11, 41:19, 41:20, 42:8, 42:12-18, 42:21, 43:2-26 and elsewhere.

Ben Sira speaks of daughters four times (7:24-25; 22:3-5; 26:10-12; 42:9-14), and always with anxiety: for her purity, her marriage, her childbearing and the family's honor. The Hebrew of 42:9-10 has the stages of a woman's life, and the Talmud's form adds a last fear, that in old age she might practice witchcraft (Sanhedrin 100b). These passages reflect a world where a daughter's marriage was arranged by her father and her conduct reflected on him (Deuteronomy 22:13-21). They are part of the book, and the Plain English Translation does not soften them. Readers may set beside them the daughters of Zelophehad (Numbers 27:1-11), Ruth, and the women who followed Jesus (Luke 8:1-3).

echoes: Leviticus 19:15; Proverbs 17:15; Exodus 21:20–27; Deuteronomy 24:3; Deuteronomy 22:13–21; Proverbs 31:10–31; Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28; Psalm 33:6; Isaiah 6:3; Deuteronomy 6:4; Psalm 139:1–12

settings.what: A father's worry over his daughter
settings.to: Fathers among his hearers, and young men who would become fathers
settings.when: At the end of the lesson on shame (41:14-42:8)
settings.why: To warn fathers to guard a daughter's honor and the family's name at each stage of her life. Knowing the hearers were men of standing in a society that measured honor by its women explains the anxiety, though not every line can be defended.
settings.readers: The Masada scroll (column IV) and manuscript B keep the passage in Hebrew, and the Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes a form of it in Ben Sira's name as one of the passages that made Rav Yosef forbid the book.
views: A judgment on women
Read alone, 42:14 is a judgment on women in general (see the note at 42:14).
Part of the worry over daughters
In the Masada scroll and the margin of manuscript B the second line of 42:14 speaks of a daughter (see the variant), which ties the saying to the father's worry in 42:9-11.

settings.what: The hymn to God's works in creation
settings.by: Ben Sira, speaking in the first person ("I will remember," 42:15)
settings.to: His pupils and the worshiping community, called at the end to praise (43:30)
settings.when: Between the book's teaching and the Praise of the Fathers (44-50)
settings.why: To lead the hearers from wonder at creation to praise of the Creator, and to prepare for the praise of God's work in Israel's history. For readers surrounded by Greek ideas that worshiped the sun and stars or called the world divine, the hymn insists that all of it is the work and servant of the one God.
settings.readers: The Masada scroll (columns V-VII) and manuscript B keep much of the hymn in Hebrew. In the church today the Catholic weekday lectionary reads 42:15-25 (Lectionary 350).

title: Sun, Moon, Snow and Sea: He Is the All
sum: The hymn moves through the sky: the clear dome, the blazing sun, the moon that marks the months and the feasts, the stars standing at their posts, and the rainbow drawn by the Most High's hands (43:1-12). Then comes the weather: snow and lightning, clouds flying from God's storehouses, thunder, hail, the north wind, frost like salt and ice like armor, and the healing dew (43:13-22).

The sea follows, calmed by God's thought and planted with islands, full of strange creatures and sea monsters, all held together by his word (43:23-26). The hymn ends in praise that can never be enough: "He is the all." He is greater than all his works; no one has seen him to describe him; we have seen only a few of his works. The Lord made all things, and he gave wisdom to the godly (43:27-33), the theme of the Praise of the Fathers that follows.
readings: Read as nature poetry

The hymn is one of the finest nature poems of ancient Israel, close to Psalm 104 and Job 38. It describes what a Judean could see: sun on the hills, rare snow, frost, dew, the sea known from sailors' tales.
Read as an argument against idolatry

Every power in the sky and the storm is God's servant. Read this way, the hymn answers the worship of sun, moon and stars that surrounded Israel (Deuteronomy 4:19), as the Wisdom of Solomon does (Wisdom of Solomon 13:1-5).
Read as a doorway to Christ
Christian readers hear in "by his word all things are put together" (43:26) and "Who has seen him?" (43:31) the questions that John 1:3, John 1:18 and Colossians 1:17 answer in Christ.

views.C: The Catechism teaches that God "can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason" (Catechism 36, quoting the First Vatican Council, Dei Filius 2). The Catechism does not cite this hymn there; setting the two side by side, with Romans 1:20 and Wisdom of Solomon 13:5, is this page's own comparison.
views.P: Protestant readers compare the hymn with Psalm 19:1-6, Psalm 104 and Psalm 147:15-18, books in every Christian Bible.
views.H: "He is the all" (43:27) sounds like the Stoic teaching that God and the world are one, but Ben Sira keeps the Creator distinct from his works (43:28).
views.J: Ben Sira's lunar calendar (43:6-8) agrees with the Temple's practice and later rabbinic Judaism, against the 364-day solar calendar of 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

deep.b: Swete prints Ἰησοῦς, "Jesus," in 43:23, from Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, which write the short sacred form ΙΣ. The sentence would then say that Jesus (the Greek form of Joshua) "planted" the deep. The Hebrew of manuscript B reads "islands" ('iyyim), and so does the Masada scroll, which keeps that word. In Greek capitals ΝΗΣΟΥΣ, "islands," and ΙΗΣΟΥΣ, "Jesus," differ by one letter. A scribe seems to have taken the first for the second and then written the name in its short form. The Latin Vulgate has "the Lord planted islands in it." The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew and the Latin, with a variant entry.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the hymn echoes Genesis 1
deep.b: My suggestion: the hymn of 42:15-43:26 echoes Genesis 1 without following it step by step. It begins with God's word (42:15, as Genesis 1:3), moves through the lights of the sky (43:2-10, day four) and ends with the creatures of the sea (43:25, day five). The fit is loose: the sun (42:16) comes before the dome of the sky (43:1), the snow, hail, lightning and frost (43:13-22) belong to no day of Genesis 1, the land and plants of day three are missing, and the rainbow (43:11-12) comes from Genesis 9:13. So the claim is only that a scribe who "digs out the wisdom of all the ancients" (39:1) begins, as Genesis does, with God's word and moves through the sky to the sea. I have not checked whether commentators have argued this.
